claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm packages Kubernetes applications as charts: directories of templated YAML manifests, a `values.yaml` file of default inputs, and metadata.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are distributed through Helm repositories and indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
The Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
Pulumi can manage any resource available in the Pulumi Registry, including AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, Cloudflare, GitHub, and Auth0, while Helm manages Kubernetes resources only.
Pulumi supports authoring infrastructure in general-purpose languages (with loops, conditionals, classes, and package management), plus YAML and HCL.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.
Helm applies resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind, defined in helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go.
Helm chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm stores release metadata as Secrets (or ConfigMaps) inside the target Kubernetes cluster.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack in a partially-updated state, and `pulumi up` reconciles toward desired state.
`helm rollback` restores a release to a previous revision recorded in release history.
Pulumi's Automation API is a programmatic SDK in every supported Pulumi language for embedding `up`, `preview`, and `destroy` in a host application.
The Helm SDK is available in Go only; other languages must shell out to the `helm` CLI.
Pulumi Policies is open source, with policy rules written in Python, TypeScript, or Open Policy Agent Rego.
Pulumi Cloud adds centralized policy management, and the Pulumi Enterprise edition adds Pulumi-maintained policy packs for CIS, PCI DSS, HITRUST, and NIST.
Helm has no native policy engine; policy is typically delegated to Kubernetes admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper.
Pulumi is open source under the Apache License 2.0.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.
The Helm docs state: "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.
Helm chart dependencies are a packaging mechanism and don't change resource ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind along with everything else.
A Helm chart can't express "install the database subchart before the application subchart" or "start this Deployment after that Job completes."

Workarounds for ordering in Helm are chart hooks ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations, whose resources Helm doesn't manage as part of the release, or application-level sequencing logic such as init containers that poll for a dependency.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts has been proposed in Helm's HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another, or setting the `dependsOn` resource option, creates an edge in the dependency graph that determines operation order.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi's parallel deployment of independent resources makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse.

`helm.v4.Chart` in the Pulumi Kubernetes provider supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm manages Kubernetes resources only; a chart can install Custom Resource Definitions, workloads, and services into a cluster, but resources outside the cluster need another tool.
The Pulumi Registry covers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, and SaaS platforms like Datadog, Auth0, GitHub, and Cloudflare.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision.
Pulumi runs through the local CLI, programmatically through the Automation API, or remotely through Pulumi Deployments.
After a failed Pulumi update, you roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns (orchestrating a production-ready cluster end-to-end, and wiring Pulumi outputs into chart values) cover most production deployments of Pulumi and Helm together.

A single Pulumi program can create the cluster (EKS, AKS, or GKE), configure networking and IAM, and install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
The Pulumi EKS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/eks/ walks through the end-to-end pattern of creating a cluster and installing the operational stack via Helm charts.

Resource outputs from a Pulumi program (such as a database connection string from `aws.rds.Instance`, a KMS key ARN, a managed Redis endpoint, or a Cloudflare zone ID) flow into a Helm chart's `values` input as typed Pulumi outputs.
Pulumi resolves chart values at deploy time and orders the chart install after the resources it depends on, so charts can consume infrastructure that did not exist when the program started.
The FAQ section "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" exists on the same page and is linked via the anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.

Pulumi's Automation API is an embeddable SDK for driving deployments from a host application such as an internal developer platform, a SaaS product, or ephemeral preview environments per pull request.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm, and they can be combined.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern for adopting Pulumi alongside Helm.
Using `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` from a Pulumi program lets you migrate from Helm incrementally.
Helm charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering them with `helm template` and converting the resulting YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option bring already-provisioned in-cluster resources under Pulumi management and generate the corresponding code.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider exposes Helm charts as first-class resources through `helm.v4.Chart` and `helm.v3.Release`.

A Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private), pass values as typed Pulumi inputs including outputs from other Pulumi resources, and manage chart lifecycle alongside other infrastructure.

`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object the chart produces as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving Helm-specific behaviors like chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges the objects from a chart and all of its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Ordering within a Helm release requires chart hooks with hook weights or logic in the application itself.
The page section "Resource ordering and dependencies" exists and is linked by the anchor #resource-ordering-and-dependencies.
Pulumi can replace Helm: teams can keep installing upstream charts from inside a Pulumi program, or move off Helm entirely by converting charts to native Pulumi code.
The page section "Adoption: coexistence, conversion, and import" exists and is linked by the anchor #adoption-coexistence-conversion-and-import.
A Pulumi Helm chart resource's `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output.
